prize_parts.citation: For showing that liquid-liquid phase separation driven by multivalent molecular interactions organises the interior of living cells into biomolecular condensates

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep biomolecular condensates as my preferred single part, with Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen. The achievement is a physical-chemical principle: weak, multivalent, reversible interactions drive demixing, and this gives a quantitative language (valency, saturation concentration, interfacial and material properties) for intracellular organisation, protein self-assembly and aggregation. Roughly fifteen years of independent in vitro reconstitution supports the principle. Hyman and Brangwynne made the founding observation with P granules and nucleoli, and Rosen's reconstitutions with defined multivalent modules showed that phase behaviour can be tuned by design, which is the step that makes it chemistry rather than cell biology. Round 1 produced no majority configuration, and the chair's summary shows B034 is held by me alone, so I do not claim it is the committee's centre of gravity. I claim it is the one candidate on the list whose core contribution is a new concept of molecular organisation, and I would accept it as one part of a two-part prize only if the three-name ceiling can be respected, which no proposed pairing currently does with B034 intact.
statement.case_against: The in vivo case remains contested. Liquid-like appearance does not by itself prove functional phase separation, overexpression artefacts are real, and critics argue the equilibrium-thermodynamics framing is too simple for a driven, active cell. The chair's questions about maturity are fair for this ballot: the demonstrations are mature, the biological consequences less so. Cutting to three names leaves out Pappu and Mittag, whose sequence-grammar and sticker-and-spacer framework is central to the physical description, and the cut is not fully principled. Support is thin (three rankings, one first place), and a prize that most colleagues rank low or not at all is hard to defend as a committee position however strong the concept.

responses.point: Aqvist makes base editing his whole prize, with Liu alone, arguing that it is a clean and chemically deep case that is distinct from the 2020 CRISPR prize because that prize honoured the programmable nuclease.
responses.response: I accept that distinction and that the Liu-alone attribution is the cleanest on the list, and the directed evolution of an adenine deaminase is real chemistry. Our disagreement is about what the Prize should weigh most. Base editing is an exceptionally good engineering of a known enzymatic reaction onto a platform the Academy recognised six years ago, and its clinical durability is still open, which you concede. I would not call it the wrong choice, but I would not put it above a prize that introduces a general principle. If the committee settles on a Liu part, I would want the citation to stay on the chemical transformation of the base and not on genome editing generally.

responses.point: Chabes argues that Crews, Deshaies and Handa join the PROTAC and cereblon-glue strands into a single principle, designable ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis, and that this is the discovery type he looks for, a mechanism turned into a general tool.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument for B007 and it moved me: the thalidomide-cereblon finding is what explains why glue and bifunctional degraders share a mechanism, so Handa's inclusion is better motivated than I allowed in round 1, when I treated the strands as separable. I still see two problems. First, the citation must then cover both strands and leaves Ciulli's structure-guided ternary-complex design uncredited, which is exactly the work that turned the idea into a rational discipline. Second, no degrader has yet reached approval. I therefore keep B007 as my first alternative and, if condensates cannot gather support, it is where I would move, not to base editing.

responses.point: Brzezinski proposes Crews and Deshaies for degraders plus Liu for base editing, presented as one part acting on proteins and one on nucleic acids, and argues that the pairing is not a double count of a single idea.
responses.response: I appreciate that this is the only configuration combining the two most widely ranked ballots, and that it is argued on mechanism rather than on counting votes. My difficulty is that the common principle he names, a chemist directing a biological machine, is a description of a field rather than a single scientific claim, so the pairing risks being a bridge between first choices more than a unified prize. It also drops Ciulli and Handa to fit the three-name cap, which is the attribution compromise the chair flagged as the least settled on the list. I would sooner see one well-attributed part than two parts built to fit the ceiling.

responses.point: Linke, as chair and a member, pairs sequencing-by-synthesis (Balasubramanian, Klenerman) with base editing (Liu), framed as reading and rewriting DNA, and ranked phase separation eighth.
responses.response: Thank you for the chair's questions, which sharpen my own position. If your eighth place reflects concern about in vivo functional evidence, I share it for the cell-level claims, but the in vitro thermodynamics is settled enough that I would call this a maturity discount and not a reason to see the field as outside chemistry. On your pairing, I think the reading-and-writing frame is attractive to a general audience, but it excludes Rothberg, Ju and Mayer from the sequencing part and the two parts then share only a substrate, not a principle. I would regard it as defensible but less convincing than either part alone.

responses.point: Aili prefers Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli for degraders, ranks phase separation fourth, and lists B034 as an alternative, noting its resonance with peptide self-assembly while flagging the in vivo relevance debate.
responses.response: I am grateful for his support in listing B034, and I agree that attribution at B007 is more convincing with Ciulli than without, since the structural and thermodynamic work on cooperativity is the reason PROTACs became a design discipline. Where I would press him is timing: he states that approval-level clinical proof for degraders is still pending, and he accepts that B034 has an in vivo gap. If we apply a similar maturity standard to both, I think the conceptual weight of condensates is not clearly lower.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards in vivo liquid-liquid phase separation as settled, or only the in vitro and conceptual framework.
Whether Pappu and Mittag should displace one of Hyman, Brangwynne or Rosen; I see no principled way to decide this beyond priority of the founding observation versus the sequence-grammar framework.
Whether B034 can attract a majority at all, since no member other than me names it in a configuration; if not, my second preference is B007, not B061.
I rely on my recollection of the literature and have not independently verified priority claims.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate. I share Lund University with Linke and Somfai, which gives no stake in any candidate. My work on lipid-protein co-assembly and amyloid is topically close to B034 and B049, and I have no known personal or institutional tie to Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu, Mittag, Cullis or Anderson. This is unchanged from round 1.
